Vision-language-action models (VLAs) fine-tune large language models (LLMs) on robot demonstrations, but how training reshapes information routing at the token level remains uncharacterized.
We present a systematic experimental framework for token-level analysis of VLAs, applying cross-instruction probes, attention analysis, Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA), and functional probes across all 32 LLM layers of OpenVLA-7B on LIBERO, with factorial trained/pretrained/untrained controls.
Three findings emerge.

Second, VLA fine-tuning front-loads instruction routing: language pretraining concentrates instruction attention at mid-depth (L9--L16, 15--22 heads), while VLA training shifts this to entry-layer routing (L0--L1: 21--25 heads) with exit-layer re-engagement (L31: 18 heads), enabling immediate instruction access ($99.6\%$ at L1 vs.\ pretrained $80.2\%$); untrained models show zero instruction-dominant heads throughout.
Third, under RSA, vision encoder geometry follows a non-monotonic trajectory through LLM layers (peak $\rho = 0.628$ at L12, declining to $0.422$ at L32), with self-supervised DINOv2 providing the highest geometric alignment ($\rho = 0.692$); this encoder ordering is metric-dependent (CKA yields different rankings; Appendix).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Vision-language-action models (VLAs) process visual observations and language instructions through a large language model to produce robot actions~\cite{brohan2023_rt2,kim2024_openvla}.
While the decoder-only architecture imposes structural constraints on information flow (the causal mask prevents image tokens from attending to subsequent instruction tokens), how VLA fine-tuning reshapes the routing and integration of multimodal information within the LLM backbone remains uncharacterized.

Recent behavioral studies reveal that VLAs rely disproportionately on visual input~\cite{grant2026}, with language instructions largely ignored by the action pathway~\cite{haon2025}.
These findings suggest internal specialization but do not explain \emph{how} instruction information reaches the action-generating readout token, \emph{what} routing strategy fine-tuning learns compared to language pretraining alone, or \emph{whether} training creates new representational structure or reconfigures inherited geometry.
Existing analyses have not combined systematic per-layer probing with factorial trained/pretrained/untrained controls, leaving the representational mechanisms of VLA fine-tuning opaque.

We address this gap by decomposing OpenVLA-7B~\cite{kim2024_openvla,karamcheti2024}, a VLA chaining a frozen DinoSigLIP vision backbone~\cite{zhai2023_siglip,oquab2024_dinov2}, an MLP projector, and Llama-2 7B~\cite{touvron2023_llama2}.
We extract representations from each of 32 LLM layers at both image-token and readout-token positions, and from external baselines (DINOv2~\cite{oquab2024_dinov2}, CLIP~\cite{radford2021_clip}).
We compare three LLM conditions (VLA-trained, pretrained Llama-2 base, and randomly initialized) crossed with instruction presence, and apply four complementary analyses: cross-instruction probes for token-level specialization, L1 attention pattern analysis for routing mechanisms, RSA~\cite{kriegeskorte2008} for geometric alignment, and MLP probes~\cite{alain2017} for functional decodability.

Three findings emerge.
\emph{First}, the VLA exhibits strict token-level functional specialization, consistent with architectural expectations: image tokens remain instruction-blind (classification at chance, $10\%$, across all 32 layers in trained, pretrained, and untrained models) due to the causal mask and frozen encoder, while the readout token maintains perfect instruction identity ($100\%$, cross-validated) from L1 onward.
\emph{Second}, VLA fine-tuning front-loads instruction routing.
Language pretraining concentrates instruction attention at mid-depth (L9--L16, 15--22 heads); VLA training shifts this to an entry-exit pattern (L0--L1: 21--25 heads, L31: 18 heads), enabling immediate instruction access ($99.6\%$ at L1 vs.\ pretrained $80.2\%$).
Untrained models show zero instruction-dominant heads at every layer.
\emph{Third}, under RSA, the LLM applies a non-monotonic transformation of vision encoder geometry: alignment peaks at L12 ($\rho = 0.628$) before declining to $0.422$ at L32, with self-supervised DINOv2 achieving the highest geometric alignment ($\rho = 0.692$); this ordering partially reverses under CKA (Appendix~\ref{sec:cka_appendix}).
Training yields non-significant geometric gain ($\Delta\rho = 0.017$, $3\%$) but substantial functional improvement at the readout token ($R^2$ $\Delta = +0.069$, $p < 0.0001$).

Our contributions are: (i)~a systematic experimental framework for token-level representational analysis of VLAs with factorial controls, verifying architecture-expected specialization between image and readout tokens; (ii)~evidence that VLA fine-tuning front-loads instruction routing, shifting it from a mid-depth pattern (inherited from language pretraining) to an entry-exit pattern with immediate instruction access, supported by causal ablation; and (iii)~the observation that, under RSA, vision encoder geometry is non-monotonically transformed by the LLM, with training primarily reshaping readout-token integration rather than visual representations (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
